Bounds on the Möbius-signed partition numbers

Taylor Daniels Address: Purdue University, West Lafayette IN
Abstract.

For n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} let Π⁡[n]\Pi[n] denote the set of partitions of nn, i.e., the set of positive integer tuples (x1,x2,…,xk)(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{k}) such that x1≥x2≥⋯≥xkx_{1}\geq x_{2}\geq\cdots\geq x_{k} and x1+x2+⋯+xk=nx_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{k}=n. Fixing f:ℕ→{0,±1}f:\mathbb{N}\to\{0,\pm 1\}, for π=(x1,x2,…,xk)∈Π⁡[n]\pi=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{k})\in\Pi[n] let f(π):=f(x1)f(x2)⋯f(xk)f(\pi):=f(x_{1})f(x_{2})\cdots f(x_{k}). In this way we define the signed partition numbers

p⁡(n,f)=∑π∈Π⁡[n]f⁡(π).p(n,f)=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi[n]}f(\pi).

Following work of Vaughan and Gafni on partitions into primes and prime powers, we derive asymptotic formulae for p⁡(n,μ)p(n,\mu) and p⁡(n,λ)p(n,\lambda), where μ\mu and λ\lambda denote the Möbius and Liouville functions from prime number theory, respectively. In addition we discuss how quantities p⁡(n,f)p(n,f) generalize the classical notion of restricted partitions.

Primary: 11P55, 11P82, 11M26.
Keywords and phrases: partitions, Möbius function, Liouville function.

1. Introduction

For n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} let Π⁡[n]\Pi[n] denote the set of partitions of nn, i.e., the set of positive integer tuples (x1,x2,…,xk)(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{k}) such that x1≥x2≥…≥xkx_{1}\geq x_{2}\geq\ldots\geq x_{k} and x1+x2+⋯+xk=nx_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{k}=n. For fixed f:ℕ→{0,±1}f:\mathbb{N}\to\{0,\pm 1\}, for n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and π=(x1,x2,…,xk)∈Π⁡[n]\pi=(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{k})\in\Pi[n] let

(1.1) f(π):=f(x1)f(x2)⋯f(xk).f(\pi):=f(x_{1})f(x_{2})\cdots f(x_{k}).

With this we define the signed partition numbers p⁡(n,f)p(n,f) via

(1.2) p⁡(n,f)=∑π∈Π⁡[n]f⁡(π).p(n,f)=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi[n]}f(\pi).

Definition (1.2) generalizes several classical partition-related quantities. For example, with the constant function 11 the p⁡(n,1)p(n,1) are the ordinary partition numbers p⁡(n)p(n), and with the indicator function 1A1_{A} for some A⊂ℕA\subset\mathbb{N} the p⁡(n,1A)p(n,1_{A}) are the AA-restricted partition numbers pA​(n)p_{A}(n), which we write as p⁡(n,A)p(n,A).

Many sequences of restricted partition numbers are classical and well studied (see, e.g., [1, 8]). Despite this, the past ten years have seen a number of new publications on the asymptotics of some restricted partition numbers, e.g., [3, 6, 9, 19].

Our two sequences (p⁡(n,f))ℕ(p(n,f))_{\mathbb{N}} of interest are those using (for ff) the Möbius μ\mu and Liouville λ\lambda functions from multiplicative number theory. If n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} has prime factorization p1a1p2a2⋯prarp_{1}^{a_{1}}p_{2}^{a_{2}}\cdots p_{r}^{a_{r}} with distinct primes pip_{i} and all ai≥1a_{i}\geq 1, then

λ⁡(n)=(−1)a1+⋯+arandμ⁡(n)={(−1)rif all ai=1,0otherwise.\lambda(n)=(-1)^{a_{1}+\cdots+a_{r}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mu(n)=\begin{cases}(-1)^{r}&\text{if all $a_{i}=1$,}\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

We note that μ⁡(n)=λ⁡(n)\mu(n)=\lambda(n) on the support of μ\mu and μ2\mu^{2}, i.e., on the set of squarefree nn.

We first state simple asymptotic results on the quantities p⁡(n,μ)p(n,\mu) and p⁡(n,λ)p(n,\lambda) which are immediate corollaries of our main results.

For all ε>0\varepsilon>0, as n→∞n\to\infty one has

We note that the results of Theorem 1.1 immediately follow from Theorems 1.2–1.5. Indeed, for the case of p⁡(n,μ)p(n,\mu), using the relations in Theorem 1.2 one may deduce that the two fractions in equation (1.11) both grow like exp⁡(n+o⁡(n))\exp(\sqrt{n}+o(\sqrt{n})), from which the bound (1.3) for p⁡(n,μ)p(n,\mu) follows at once. Because (−1)−x=+1(-1)^{-x}=+1 when x=2​kx=2k with k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, the asymptotic relation for log⁡p⁡(2​k,μ)\log p(2k,\mu) in (1.4) similarly follows at once. The statements concerning p⁡(n,λ)p(n,\lambda) and log⁡p⁡(2​k,λ)\log p(2k,\lambda) similarly follow from Theorems 1.4 and 1.5.

We now discuss three classical results on certain sequences (p⁡(n,A))ℕ(p(n,A))_{\mathbb{N}} to help contextualize the relations of Theorem 1.1. The most well known of these is the relation

log⁡p⁡(n,1)∼κ​n,\log p(n,1)\sim\kappa\sqrt{n},

where

κ:=π​2/3,\kappa:=\pi\sqrt{2/3},

which is an immediate corollary of Hardy and Ramanujan’s main results in [12].

Before stating the second result, we recall that A⊂ℕA\subset\mathbb{N} is said to have density δA\delta_{A} if the ratio |A∩{1,2,…,N}|​N−1|A\cap\{1,2,\ldots,N\}|N^{-1} tends to δA\delta_{A} as N→∞N\to\infty. It is evident that δℕ=1\delta_{\mathbb{N}}=1, and it is well known that the set of squarefree numbers has density 6/π2≈0.6016/\pi^{2}\approx 0.601. The prime number theorem implies that δℙ=0\delta_{\mathbb{P}}=0. A remarkable theorem of Erdős [8] states that: if A⊂ℕA\subset\mathbb{N} and gcd⁡(A)=1\mathrm{gcd}(A)=1, then AA has density δA>0\delta_{A}>0 if and only if

(1.14) log⁡p⁡(n,A)∼κ​δA​n.\log p(n,A)\sim\kappa\sqrt{\delta_{A}n}.

We remark that the proof of the “only if” statement in Erdős’ theorem is omitted in [8] since the proof of a similar result is given there, and that a complete proof of both statements may be found in [14]*Ch. 16. The third result, though originally due to Roth and Szekeres [16], can be deduced as a corollary to Vaughan’s formula (1.10). Namely, as n→∞n\to\infty one has

(1.15) log⁡p⁡(n,ℙ)∼κ​2​nlog⁡n.\log p(n,\mathbb{P})\sim\kappa\sqrt{\frac{2n}{\log n}}.

Noting that κ=2​ζ⁡(2)=2​𝔷\kappa=2\sqrt{\zeta(2)}=2\sqrt{\mathfrak{z}}, Theorem 1.1 states that as n→∞n\to\infty one has

p⁡(n,μ)=O⁡(e(1+ε)​n)andp⁡(n,λ)=O⁡(e(12+ε)​κ​n),p(n,\mu)=O(e^{(1+\varepsilon)\sqrt{n}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad p(n,\lambda)=O(e^{(\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon)\kappa\sqrt{n}}),

and that for n=2​kn=2k one has

log⁡p⁡(2​k,μ)∼2​kandlog⁡p⁡(2​k,λ)∼12​κ​2​k.\log p(2k,\mu)\sim\sqrt{2k}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\log p(2k,\lambda)\sim\tfrac{1}{2}\kappa\sqrt{2k}.

Finally we comment on our use of the term “signed partition number”, since it is apparent from (1.1) and (1.2) that “weighted partition number” is an equally appropriate term for p⁡(n,f)p(n,f). We avoid this latter term due to its ubiquity in the literature as a moniker for sequences having generating functions of the form

(1.16) Φ⁡(z)=∏n=1∞(1−zn)−f⁡(n)=1+∑n=1∞pf​(n)​zn\Phi(z)=\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}(1-z^{n})^{-f(n)}=1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}p_{f}(n)z^{n}

for some nonnegative integer-valued f⁡(n)f(n). These pf​(n)p_{f}(n) coincide with our p⁡(n,f)p(n,f) if ff takes only the values 00 and 11, but given the different roles f⁡(n)f(n) plays in (1.5) and (1.16), we favor the descriptor “signed” for p⁡(n,f)p(n,f) rather than “weighted.”

2. Notation and structure

Expressions O⁡(g⁡(x))O(g(x)) with g⁡(x)>0g(x)>0 are quantities bounded by some constant multiple of g⁡(x)g(x). Let 1≤Q≤X1\leq Q\leq X. If 0≤a≤q0\leq a\leq q and (a,q)=1(a,q)=1, we define the arc about a/qa/q as the set

Among the sets 𝔐⁡(a/q)\mathfrak{M}(a/q), the major arcs are those 𝔐⁡(a/q)\mathfrak{M}(a/q) with q≤Qq\leq Q, and 𝔐⁡(X,Q)\mathfrak{M}(X,Q) denotes the union of all major arcs. Ultimately, only α\alpha lying in small subsets of the arcs 𝔐⁡(0/1)\mathfrak{M}(0/1), 𝔐⁡(1/2)\mathfrak{M}(1/2), and 𝔐⁡(1/1)\mathfrak{M}(1/1) significantly contribute to the integral (1.8), with all other α\alpha contributing to an error term. Anticipating this, for X,X∗>1X,X_{*}>1 we define

𝔓\displaystyle\mathfrak{P} ={α∈[0,1):‖α‖≤X−1​(log⁡X)−14},\displaystyle=\{\alpha\in[0,1):\|\alpha\|\leq X^{-1}(\log X)^{-\frac{1}{4}}\},
𝔓∗\displaystyle\mathfrak{P}_{*} ={α∈[0,1):|α−12|≤X∗−1​(log⁡X∗)−14}.\displaystyle=\{\alpha\in[0,1):|\alpha-\tfrac{1}{2}|\leq X_{*}^{-1}(\log X_{*})^{-\frac{1}{4}}\}.

Following Gafni [10] we term the sets 𝔓\mathfrak{P} and 𝔓∗\mathfrak{P}_{*} the principal arcs, though colloquially the terms “super-major arcs” and “major-major arcs” have also been used.

Functions Φ⁡(z,f)\Phi(z,f), Ψ⁡(z,f)\Psi(z,f), etc. are simply written as Φ⁡(z)\Phi(z), Ψ⁡(z)\Psi(z), etc. when the ff used is clear or when the discussions apply to general f:ℕ→{0,±1}f:\mathbb{N}\to\{0,\pm 1\}. For ρ,ρ∗∈(0,1)\rho,\rho_{*}\in(0,1) it is convenient to write

(2.1) X=1log⁡(1/ρ)andX∗=1log⁡(1/ρ∗),X=\frac{1}{\log(1/\rho)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad X_{*}=\frac{1}{\log(1/\rho_{*})},

so that

(2.2) ρ=e−1/Xandρ∗=e−1/X∗,\rho=e^{-1/X}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\rho_{*}=e^{-1/X_{*}},

and this convention is maintained throughout this paper.

Structure

This paper has three major components. Section 3 provides a general recipe for our analyses, after which sections 4–7 consider the quantities Ψ⁡(ρ​e​(α),μ)\Psi(\rho e(\alpha),\mu) when α\alpha is in the minor, major, and principal arcs and ρ\rho is sufficiently close to 11 (rather, when XX is sufficiently large). In section 8 we examine the implicit relationships between ρ\rho, XX, and xx when xx is large and ρ=ρ⁡(x)\rho=\rho(x) is defined as the (unique) solution to equation (sp). Similar analyses are made for ρ∗\rho_{*} and X∗X_{*} with ρ∗\rho_{*} defined as the solution to (sp ∗ ), concluding the proof of Theorem 1.2.

Using our results on Ψ⁡(z,μ)\Psi(z,\mu), sections 9 and 10 establish that only those α\alpha in the principal arcs significantly contribute to the integral (1.8) for p⁡(x,μ)p(x,\mu). Following this, section 11 treats these principal-arc integrals to ultimately establish Theorem 1.3.

Finally, section 12 considers the quantities p⁡(x,λ)p(x,\lambda). Because the Liouville λ\lambda function is far easier to handle than the Möbius μ\mu function, the techniques of sections 3–8 allow for a rapid analysis of Ψ⁡(z,λ)\Psi(z,\lambda) and proof of Theorem 1.4. Due to the overwhelming similarities of the relations of Theorems 1.2 and 1.4, the arguments of sections 9–11 that prove Theorem 1.3 allow for an almost-immediate proof of Theorem 1.5.

A note on ρ∗\rho_{*} and X∗X_{*}

In sections 3–7 our results involve only ρ\rho and XX, and not ρ∗\rho_{*} and X∗X_{*}. Indeed, until section 8 our results do not require that ρ\rho (or ρ∗\rho_{*}) be a solution to equation (sp) (or (sp ∗ )), so there is no need to discuss two different ρ,ρ∗∈(0,1)\rho,\rho_{*}\in(0,1) until then. Moreover, in section 8 we find that when ρ\rho and ρ∗\rho_{*} are the (unique) solutions to (sp) and (sp ∗ ), respectively, one has X∼X∗∼2​xX\sim X_{*}\sim 2\sqrt{x}, making the results of sections 3–7 equally applicable if one uses ρ∗\rho_{*} and X∗X_{*} in place of ρ\rho and XX, respectively.

3. A template for our analyses

Our analyses of Ψ⁡(z,μ)\Psi(z,\mu) and Ψ⁡(z,λ)\Psi(z,\lambda) for z=ρ​e​(α)z=\rho e(\alpha) with α\alpha in the sets 𝔐⁡(X,Q)\mathfrak{M}(X,Q) and 𝔪⁡(X,Q)\mathfrak{m}(X,Q) more or less follow the same sequence of steps. This section outlines these steps and summarizes them in Lemma 3.4.

By comparison with Ψ⁡(z,1)\Psi(z,1), the double series for Ψ⁡(z,f)\Psi(z,f) in equation (1.6) converges absolutely for |z|<1|z|<1. Thus, we exchange the sums in (1.6) and define

Fk​(z)=∑n=1∞fk​(n)​znF_{k}(z)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f^{k}(n)z^{n}

so that

Ψ⁡(z)=∑k=1∞∑n=1∞fk​(n)k​zn​k=∑k=1∞1k​Fk​(zk).\Psi(z)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{f^{k}(n)}{k}z^{nk}=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k}F_{k}(z^{k}).

A cornerstone of our analyses is the observation that if f⁡(n)f(n) only takes values 00 or ±1\pm 1, then the functions Fk​(z)F_{k}(z) are only unique up to the parity of kk. Indeed, as fk​(n)=f​(n)f^{k}(n)=f(n) for odd kk and fk​(n)=f2​(n)=|f⁡(n)|f^{k}(n)=f^{2}(n)=|f(n)| for even kk, we see that Fk​(z)=Fk⁡(mod​ 2)​(z)F_{k}(z)=F_{k\,\,(\mathrm{mod}\,2)}(z) for all kk. We thus let

(3.1) F0​(z)\displaystyle F_{0}(z) =∑n=1∞f2​(n)​zn,\displaystyle=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f^{2}(n)z^{n},\qquad F1​(z)=∑n=1∞f⁡(n)​zn,\displaystyle F_{1}(z)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f(n)z^{n},
(3.2) Ψ0​(z)\displaystyle\Psi_{0}(z) =∑k≡0​(2)1k​F0​(zk),\displaystyle=\sum_{k\equiv 0\,(2)}\frac{1}{k}F_{0}(z^{k}),\qquad Ψ1​(z)=∑k≡1​(2)1k​F1​(zk),\displaystyle\Psi_{1}(z)=\sum_{k\equiv 1\,(2)}\frac{1}{k}F_{1}(z^{k}),

so that

Ψ⁡(z)=Ψ0​(z)+Ψ1​(z).\Psi(z)=\Psi_{0}(z)+\Psi_{1}(z).
Remark 3.1.

We write F0​(z)F_{0}(z) instead of F2​(z)F_{2}(z) because the sums ∑nf2​(n)​zn\sum_{n}f^{2}(n)z^{n} provide the main asymptotic terms in our analyses of p⁡(n,μ)p(n,\mu) and p⁡(n,λ)p(n,\lambda).

For j∈{0,1}j\in\{0,1\} we split the functions Ψj​(z)\Psi_{j}(z) into leading sums and tail sums, namely

(3.3) Ψj​(z)=∑k≤Kk≡j⁡(2)1k​Fj​(zk)+∑k>Kk≡j⁡(2)1k​Fj​(zk),\Psi_{j}(z)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\leq K\\ k\equiv j\,(2)\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{k}F_{j}(z^{k})+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k>K\\ k\equiv j\,(2)\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{k}F_{j}(z^{k}),

where K>1K>1 is a real parameter of our choosing. The tail sums in equation (3.3) are always part of our error terms, so we record the following lemma bounding these tail sums independently of jj, and even independently of ff.

Lemma 3.2.

Let f:ℕ→{0,±1}f:\mathbb{N}\to\{0,\pm 1\}. For real α\alpha and large XX and KK one has that

∑k>K1k​Fk​(ρk​e​(k​α))≪XK.\sum_{k>K}\frac{1}{k}F_{k}(\rho^{k}e(k\alpha))\ll\frac{X}{K}.
Proof.

For fixed kk we see that

Fk​(ρk​e​(k​α))=∑n=1∞fk​(n)​ρn​k​e​(n​k​α)≪∑n=1∞ρn​k=ρk1−ρk.F_{k}(\rho^{k}e(k\alpha))=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}f^{k}(n)\rho^{nk}e(nk\alpha)\ll\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\rho^{nk}=\frac{\rho^{k}}{1-\rho^{k}}.

∑k>K1k​Fk​(ρk​e​(k​α))≪∑k>K1k​e−k/X1−e−k/X=∑k>K1/kek/X−1≪∑k>KXk2,\sum_{k>K}\frac{1}{k}F_{k}(\rho^{k}e(k\alpha))\ll\sum_{k>K}\frac{1}{k}\,\frac{e^{-k/X}}{1-e^{-k/X}}=\sum_{k>K}\frac{1/k}{e^{k/X}-1}\ll\sum_{k>K}\frac{X}{k^{2}},

and the result follows. ∎

The analyses of Ψ0​(z)\Psi_{0}(z) and Ψ1​(z)\Psi_{1}(z) are thus reduced to analyses of F0​(zk)F_{0}(z^{k}) and F1​(zk)F_{1}(z^{k}) for k≤Kk\leq K. in place of (3.5). The above discussions are summarized in the following lemma.

Lemma 3.4.

Let f:ℕ→{0,±1}f:\mathbb{N}\to\{0,\pm 1\}, and for j∈{0,1}j\in\{0,1\} let Fj​(z)F_{j}(z) and Ψj​(z)\Psi_{j}(z) be defined as in (3.1) and (3.2), so that

Ψj​(z)≪𝒳j​(z)+X/K(z∈Ω).\Psi_{j}(z)\ll\mathcal{X}_{j}(z)+X/K\qquad(z\in\Omega).

4. The minor arcs

We now begin our specific analyses of Ψ⁡(z,μ)\Psi(z,\mu), so Ψ⁡(z)\Psi(z) always indicates Ψ⁡(z,μ)\Psi(z,\mu) unless otherwise stated. As Ψ1​(z)\Psi_{1}(z) is easier to estimate than Ψ0​(z)\Psi_{0}(z), we analyze Ψ1​(z)\Psi_{1}(z) first.

Lemma 4.1.

Fix A>0A>0. For X>X0​(A)X>X_{0}(A) and α∈𝔪⁡(X,Q)\alpha\in\mathfrak{m}(X,Q) one has

Ψ1​(ρ​e​(α))≪X​(log⁡X)−A.\Psi_{1}(\rho e(\alpha))\ll X(\log X)^{-A}.
Proof.

With f=μf=\mu, the function F1​(z)F_{1}(z) of (3.1) is ∑n=1∞μ⁡(n)​zn\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu(n)z^{n}, whereby

Ψ1(ρe(α))=∑k≡1​(2)1kF1(ρke(kα))=∑k≡1​(2)1k∑n=1∞μ(n)e−nk/Xe(nkα).\Psi_{1}(\rho e(\alpha))=\sum_{k\equiv 1\,(2)}\frac{1}{k}F_{1}(\rho^{k}e(k\alpha))=\sum_{k\equiv 1\,(2)}\frac{1}{k}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mu(n)e^{-nk/X}e(nk\alpha).

(4.2) Sμ​(t,θ)≪t​(log⁡t)−Afor t≥3, uniformly in θ.S_{\mu}(t,\theta)\ll t(\log t)^{-A}\qquad\text{for $t\geq 3$, uniformly in $\theta$.}

Trivially bounding Sμ​(t,k​α)≪tS_{\mu}(t,k\alpha)\ll t when t<X3/4/kt<X^{3/4}/k, it follows that integral (4.1) is

≪kX[∫0X3/4​k−1e−tk/Xtdt+∫X3/4​k−1∞e−tk/Xt(logt)−Adt]\displaystyle\ll\frac{k}{X}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\int_{0}^{X^{3/4}k^{-1}}e^{-tk/X}t\,dt+\int_{X^{3/4}k^{-1}}^{\infty}e^{-tk/X}t(\log t)^{-A}\,dt}}\right]
(4.3) ≪Xk[∫0X−1/4e−uudu+log−A(X3/4k−1)∫X−1/4∞e−uudu],\displaystyle\ll\frac{X}{k}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\int_{0}^{X^{-1/4}}e^{-u}u\,du+\log^{-A}(X^{3/4}k^{-1})\int_{X^{-1/4}}^{\infty}e^{-u}u\,du}}\right],

and we note that the assumption k≤X1/2k\leq X^{1/2} ensures that our use of inequality (4.2) remains valid as X→∞X\to\infty. We also note the change of k/Xk/X to X/kX/k in expression (4.3). As ∫0ae−u​u​𝑑u≪a\int_{0}^{a}e^{-u}u\,du\ll a and ∫a∞e−u​u​𝑑u≪1\int_{a}^{\infty}e^{-u}u\,du\ll 1 when 0<a<10<a<1, we deduce that

Fk​(ρk​e​(k​α))≪Xk​[X−14+log−A⁡(X34​k−1)]≪X/k(log⁡X)A(k≤X12).F_{k}(\rho^{k}e(k\alpha))\ll\frac{X}{k}\Big[X^{-\frac{1}{4}}+\log^{-A}(X^{\frac{3}{4}}k^{-1})\Big]\ll\frac{X/k}{(\log X)^{A}}\qquad(k\leq X^{\frac{1}{2}}).

Remark 4.2.

The reader may notice that the proof of Lemma 4.1 did not utilize the assumption that α∈𝔪⁡(X,Q)\alpha\in\mathfrak{m}(X,Q). Indeed, because Davenport’s inequality (4.2) is uniform in the variable θ\theta (which became k​αk\alpha above), we immediately deduce the following corollary.

Ψ1​(ρ​e​(α))≪X​(log⁡X)−A.\Psi_{1}(\rho e(\alpha))\ll X(\log X)^{-A}.

The analysis of Ψ0​(ρ​e​(α))\Psi_{0}(\rho e(\alpha)) is much more involved than that of Ψ1​(ρ​e​(α))\Psi_{1}(\rho e(\alpha)), as we require a suitable replacement for Davenport’s inequality (4.2) for the sums Sμ2​(t,θ)S_{\mu^{2}}(t,\theta). If 1≤Q≤X3/71\leq Q\leq X^{3/7}, then

Suppose for the moment that KK, 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} are quantities such that {k​α}∈𝔪⁡(𝒳,𝒬)\{k\alpha\}\in\mathfrak{m}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Q}) for all α∈𝔪⁡(X,Q)\alpha\in\mathfrak{m}(X,Q) and all k≤Kk\leq K. In this case we have (for a general ff) that

(4.5) supα∈𝔪⁡(X,Q)k≤K|Sf​(t,k​α)|=supα∈𝔪⁡(X,Q)k≤K|Sf​(t,{k​α})|≤supθ∈𝔪⁡(𝒳,𝒬)|Sf​(t,θ)|.\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in\mathfrak{m}(X,Q)\\ k\leq K\end{subarray}}|S_{f}(t,k\alpha)|=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in\mathfrak{m}(X,Q)\\ k\leq K\end{subarray}}|S_{f}(t,\{k\alpha\})|\leq\sup_{\theta\in\mathfrak{m}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Q})}|S_{f}(t,\theta)|.

Next, considering the definitions of the sets 𝔐⁡(𝒳,𝒬)\mathfrak{M}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Q}) and 𝔪⁡(𝒳,𝒬)\mathfrak{m}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Q}), one sees that if t≥𝒳t\geq\mathcal{X}, then 𝔪⁡(𝒳,𝒬)⊂𝔪⁡(t,𝒬)\mathfrak{m}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Q})\subset\mathfrak{m}(t,\mathcal{Q}). From (4.5) then, for all t≥𝒳t\geq\mathcal{X} we have that

(4.6) supα∈𝔪⁡(X,Q)k≤K|Sf​(t,k​α)|≤supθ∈𝔪⁡(𝒳,𝒬)|Sf​(t,θ)|≤supθ∈𝔪⁡(t,𝒬)|Sf​(t,θ)|.\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in\mathfrak{m}(X,Q)\\ k\leq K\end{subarray}}|S_{f}(t,k\alpha)|\leq\sup_{\theta\in\mathfrak{m}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Q})}|S_{f}(t,\theta)|\leq\sup_{\theta\in\mathfrak{m}(t,\mathcal{Q})}|S_{f}(t,\theta)|.

Suppose that 1≤Q≤X1\leq Q\leq X, that 1≤𝒬≤𝒳3/71\leq\mathcal{Q}\leq\mathcal{X}^{3/7}, that K>0K>0, and that: For all α∈𝔪⁡(X,Q)\alpha\in\mathfrak{m}(X,Q) and k≤Kk\leq K one has {k​α}∈𝔪⁡(𝒳,𝒬)\{k\alpha\}\in\mathfrak{m}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Q}). Then for t≥𝒳t\geq\mathcal{X} one has

(4.7) supα∈𝔪⁡(X,Q)k≤K|Sμ2​(t,k​α)|≤supθ∈𝔪⁡(t,𝒬)|Sμ2​(t,θ)|≪t1+ε​𝒬−1.\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in\mathfrak{m}(X,Q)\\ k\leq K\end{subarray}}|S_{\mu^{2}}(t,k\alpha)|\leq\sup_{\theta\in\mathfrak{m}(t,\mathcal{Q})}|S_{\mu^{2}}(t,\theta)|\ll t^{1+\varepsilon}\mathcal{Q}^{-1}.

We now consider how to select KK, 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. The simple choices 𝒳=X\mathcal{X}=X and 𝒬=Q\mathcal{Q}=Q yield the estimate Ψ⁡(ρ​e​(α))≪X1+ε\Psi(\rho e(\alpha))\ll X^{1+\varepsilon}, which is insufficient since Ψ⁡(ρ​e​(α))\Psi(\rho e(\alpha)) is comparable to XX when α∈𝔐⁡(X,Q)\alpha\in\mathfrak{M}(X,Q). Examining Lemma 4.4 and the proof of Lemma 4.1, one may deduce that decreasing 𝒳\mathcal{X} has a far greater effect on the resulting estimates of Ψ0​(ρ​e​(α))\Psi_{0}(\rho e(\alpha)) than does increasing 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, so we prioritize decreasing 𝒳\mathcal{X}. The mechanism of this exchange is shown in the following lemma.

Lemma 4.6.

Fix κ∈(0,1)\kappa\in(0,1), let 1≤Q≤X1\leq Q\leq X, let α∈𝔪⁡(X,Q)\alpha\in\mathfrak{m}(X,Q), and let 1≤k≤Qκ1\leq k\leq Q^{\kappa}. If (ak,qk)=1(a_{k},q_{k})=1 and

(4.8) |qkkα−ak|≤Q1−κ/X,\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|q_{k}k\alpha-a_{k}}}\right|\leq Q^{1-\kappa}/X,

then qk>Q1−κq_{k}>Q^{1-\kappa}. In particular one has {k​α}∈𝔪⁡(X,Q1−κ)\{k\alpha\}\in\mathfrak{m}(X,Q^{1-\kappa}). Finally, if 0<ν<1−κ0<\nu<1-\kappa then

Before proceeding further we must address a technical issue introduced by this “arc transference” in equation (9.3). Because ρ⁡(x)\rho(x) and ρ∗​(x)\rho_{*}(x) are unlikely to be equal, so then are XX and X∗X_{*} unlikely to be equal. Thus, the division of [0,1)[0,1) into major, minor, and principal arcs using XX and QQ (which is a power of XX) is now problematic. In particular, we must define “∗*-arcs” using X∗X_{*} and Q∗Q_{*} via

𝔐∗​(a/q):={α∈[0,1):|α−a/q|≤Q∗/(q​X∗)},\mathfrak{M}_{*}(a/q):=\{\alpha\in[0,1):|\alpha-a/q|\leq Q_{*}/(qX_{*})\},

Fortunately, this technicality does not create much trouble. 12. Formulae for p⁡(x,λ)p(x,\lambda)

Given the functions’ strong connection, results for one of Möbius’ μ\mu and Liouville’s λ\lambda functions are often easily translated into results for the other. Our formulae for p⁡(x,μ)p(x,\mu) and p⁡(x,λ)p(x,\lambda) conform to this pattern. Many of the proofs of our lemmata for p⁡(x,λ)p(x,\lambda) are nearly identical to the corresponding ones for p⁡(x,μ)p(x,\mu), and indeed often easier since λ2​(n)=1\lambda^{2}(n)=1 for all nn, so our analyses in this section are notably briefer than those of the previous sections.

While the sets 𝔐⁡(X,Q)\mathfrak{M}(X,Q), 𝔪⁡(X,Q)\mathfrak{m}(X,Q), 𝔓\mathfrak{P}, and 𝔓∗\mathfrak{P}_{*} are all defined as in section 2, our choice of QQ for p⁡(x,λ)p(x,\lambda) is not the same as it is for p⁡(x,μ)p(x,\mu), so we start anew with an unknown QQ such that 1≤Q≤X1\leq Q\leq X. All other notations are also maintained, but we emphasize that Φ⁡(z)\Phi(z) and Ψ⁡(z)\Psi(z) now denote Φ⁡(z,λ)\Phi(z,\lambda) and Ψ⁡(z,λ)\Psi(z,\lambda), respectively. In particular, equations (sp) and (sp ∗ ) are still written as Ψ(1)​(ρ)=x\Psi_{(1)}(\rho)=x and Ψ(1)​(−ρ)=x\Psi_{(1)}(-\rho)=x. As done in our analysis of Ψ⁡(ρ​e​(α),μ)\Psi(\rho e(\alpha),\mu), in analyzing Ψ⁡(ρ​e​(α),λ)\Psi(\rho e(\alpha),\lambda) we do not assume ρ\rho to be a solution to (sp) or (sp ∗ ) until necessary.

Finally we note that the functions F0​(z)F_{0}(z) and F1​(z)F_{1}(z) of (3.1) are now given by the formulae

F0​(z)=∑n=1∞znandF1​(z)=∑n=1∞λ⁡(n)​zn.F_{0}(z)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}z^{n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad F_{1}(z)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\lambda(n)z^{n}.
